articles.title: Democratic Socialists on the Rise: Darializa Avila Chevalier & Claire Valdez Set to Win House Seats
articles.content_excerpt: New York City is preparing to send two DSA members, presumptive election night winners Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, to Capitol Hill. DSA -backed candidates made historic gains in this year’s Democratic primaries, with at least five expected to join current DSA members Rashida Tlaib and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in the House. But can socialism really make headway in the halls of Congress? Democracy Now! fellows Amba Guerguerian and Diego Ramos report. “Our task is going to be winning our colleagues over to our position and finding common ground,” Valdez tells Democracy Now! “Some of the most popular policies in our country’s history have been socialist policies,” says Avila Chevalier. “They have been the things that working people have organized for and won.”

articles.title: Latino Voters Swing Away from Trump for “Terrorizing Our Communities”: Marisa Franco of Mijente
articles.content_excerpt: In 2024, Donald Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Hispanic voters, suggesting that a major realignment in party preferences might be underway. But just two years later, it appears much of that support has eroded. Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters say they will now support Democrats in the midterms, including 11% who previously had voted for President Trump. We get a bird’s-eye view of what to expect from the Latino vote from Marisa Franco, the co-founder and director of the advocacy organization Mijente. articles.title: Students Celebrate Lula’s Victory and Denounce Violence Against Indigenous Peoples
articles.content_excerpt: One week after the historic victory of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of the 2026 elections, the National Union of Students is holding nationwide mobilizations this Sunday, November 1. The rallies were titled “Brazil with an ‘S’” (“Brasil com S”). The actions came in response to statements made by supporters of defeated far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who questioned the election results. Beyond celebrating Lula’s win, the mobilizations also denounced and condemned the attacks against Indigenous peoples following the election. According to Brazil’s largest Indigenous organization, the Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil, APIB, there have been more than 30 reports of violence against Indigenous individuals since the election. articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content_excerpt: Hundreds participated in a solidarity rally in Lahore, Pakistan, earlier this week, demanding an end to the oppressive decades-long US blockade and sanctions on Cuba and denouncing its targeting of Raul Castro, leader of the Cuban revolution and former president. articles.title: War in Africa: the political economy of the richest continent in the world
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content_excerpt: Mainstream news has rediscovered Africa, and it is recycling old narratives: armed conflict, state collapse, and humanitarian catastrophe. Tigray is at war again. Darfur and Kordofan bleed under the Rapid Support Forces. M23 carves up eastern Congo. Northern Mozambique is still emptying its villages. Across the Sahel, jihadist attacks and blockades strangle whole towns, and Somalia’s war grinds on into its fourth decade. All of this is real. People are dying, and millions are displaced. But why is the story always told the same way it was told in the 1990s and early 2000s, as a continent of chaos and hunger, a cautionary tale, an example of what not to be? articles.title: Across the Red Sea, the wars feed each other
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content_excerpt: Sudan’s war is usually described as an African catastrophe, Yemen’s as an Arabian conflict, and the war around Iran as a Gulf crisis. Such divisions obscure the movement of weapons, money, soldiers, and commercial interests between them. Look from Africa’s Red Sea coast, and another picture emerges. These wars have distinct origins, but they increasingly sustain one another through military patronage, competition over ports, and the destruction of civilian livelihoods. The starting point must be Sudan’s people. The World Food Program currently estimates that 19.5 million face acute hunger, while around 8.6 million are internally displaced.
